chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: Between three and four in the afternoon, Prince Andrew—who had kept pressing Kutuzov for permission—arrived at Grunth and reported to Bagration. Bonaparte's aide-de-camp hadn't yet reached Murat's forces, and the battle hadn't begun. In Bagration's detachment, nobody had any clear picture of the larger situation. Some spoke of peace but didn't really believe it was possible; others talked about a battle but didn't believe it was actually imminent. Bagration, knowing that Bolkonsky was one of Kutuzov's favorite and trusted adjutants, received him with special respect, explaining that there would probably be an engagement that day or the next, and giving him full freedom to either stay through the battle or join the rearguard and oversee the order of retreat, "which is also very important."
"In any case, there probably won't be a battle today," said Bagration, as if to put Prince Andrew at ease.

"If he's just one of those polished staff officers hunting for a medal, he can earn it just as easily in the rearguard. But if he wants to stay with me, let him—he'll be useful here if he's a brave officer," Bagration thought. Without replying, Prince Andrew asked the prince's permission to ride around the position and survey the troop dispositions, so he'd have his bearings in case he needed to carry out an order. The officer on duty—a handsome, elegantly dressed man with a diamond ring on his finger, who liked speaking French despite doing it badly—volunteered to show Prince Andrew around.
Everywhere they looked, they saw rain-soaked officers with dejected faces who seemed to be searching for something, and soldiers dragging doors, benches, and fencing out of the village.

"There, you see, Prince? We can't keep those men in line," said the staff officer, pointing at the soldiers. "The officers have no control over them. And there"—he pointed at a sutler's tent—"they crowd in and sit down. I cleared them all out this morning, and look, it's packed again. I need to go over there and put some fear into them, Prince. It'll only take a moment."
"Sure, let's go in. I'll grab a roll and some cheese," said Prince Andrew, who hadn't had a chance to eat anything yet.
"Why didn't you say so, Prince? I would have offered you something."
They dismounted and went into the tent. Several officers with flushed, weary faces sat at a table, eating and drinking.

"Now what is this, gentlemen?" said the staff officer in the scolding tone of someone who has repeated the same thing too many times. "You know you can't just leave your posts like this. The prince ordered that no one is to leave his position. And you, Captain"—he turned to a thin, dirty little artillery officer who, bootless (he'd given them to the canteen keeper to dry), was standing in just his stockings and rose with an awkward smile when they entered.

"Aren't you ashamed of yourself, Captain Tushin?" he continued. "You'd think an artillery officer would set a better example, and here you are without your boots! When the alarm sounds, you'll look pretty foolish without them!" The staff officer allowed himself a smile. "Please return to your posts, gentlemen—all of you!" he added in a commanding tone.

Prince Andrew couldn't help smiling as he looked at Captain Tushin, who stood there silent and smiling, shifting from one stockinged foot to the other, glancing up with his large, intelligent, kindly eyes, looking from Prince Andrew to the staff officer and back.

"The soldiers say it's easier to walk without boots," Tushin offered with a shy smile, clearly trying for a lighthearted tone. But before he'd finished, he sensed that the joke had fallen flat. He turned red with embarrassment.
"Please return to your posts," said the staff officer, trying to maintain his serious expression.
Prince Andrew glanced once more at the little artillery officer's figure. There was something distinctive about him—completely unsoldierly, almost comical, but deeply appealing.
The staff officer and Prince Andrew mounted up and rode on.

Riding beyond the village, constantly meeting and overtaking soldiers and officers from various regiments, they saw on their left some entrenchments being dug, the freshly turned clay showing red against the ground. Several battalions of soldiers in their shirtsleeves, despite the cold wind, swarmed over these earthworks like white ants; shovelfuls of red clay kept flying up from behind the embankment, thrown by unseen hands. Prince Andrew and the officer rode up, inspected the entrenchments, and moved on. Just behind these works they came upon several dozen soldiers, constantly being replaced by others running from the trench. They had to hold their noses and spur their horses to a trot to escape the poisonous stench of the latrines.
[speaking in French] "There you have the pleasures of camp life, Prince," said the staff officer.
* "These are the pleasures of camp life, Prince."
They rode up the opposite hill. From there, the French were already visible. Prince Andrew stopped and began studying the position.
"That's our battery," said the staff officer, pointing to the highest ground. "It's commanded by that odd fellow we saw without his boots. You can see everything from up there—let's go, Prince."
"Thank you very much, but I'll go on alone," said Prince Andrew, wanting to be rid of the staff officer's company. "Please don't trouble yourself any further."
The staff officer stayed behind, and Prince Andrew rode on alone.

The further forward he went and the closer to the enemy, the more orderly and cheerful the troops became. The worst disorder and gloom had been in the baggage train he'd passed that morning on the Znaim road, seven miles from the French. At Grunth too, you could sense some anxiety and unease. But the closer Prince Andrew came to the French lines, the more confident the troops appeared. The soldiers in their greatcoats stood in formation, the sergeants and company officers were counting heads, poking the last man in each section in the ribs and telling him to raise his hand. Soldiers scattered across the area were dragging logs and brushwood, building shelters with cheerful chatter and laughter. Around campfires, men sat dressed and undressed, drying their shirts and leg wraps or mending boots and overcoats, crowding around the stew pots and porridge cookers. In one company, dinner was ready, and the soldiers watched the steaming pot eagerly, waiting for a sample—which a quartermaster sergeant was carrying in a wooden bowl to an officer sitting on a log outside his shelter—to be tasted and approved.

Another company, a lucky one since not every unit had vodka, was gathered around a pockmarked, broad-shouldered sergeant major who tilted a small keg, filling one by one the canteen lids held out to him. The soldiers raised the lids to their lips with something like reverence, drained them, swished the vodka around in their mouths, and walked away with brightened faces, licking their lips and wiping them on the sleeves of their greatcoats. Every face was as calm as if all this were happening back home during a peaceful camp, not within sight of the enemy before a battle in which at least half of them would fall. After passing a chasseur regiment and the Kiev grenadiers—fine men busy with similar peaceful routines—near the regimental commander's shelter, which was taller and different from the rest, Prince Andrew came upon a platoon of grenadiers in front of whom a naked man lay on the ground. Two soldiers held him down while two others lashed his bare back with switches. The man screamed in an unnatural, animal way. A bullet had clearly not caused this—it was punishment. A heavy-set major paced up and down the line, ignoring the screams, and kept repeating:
"It's a disgrace for a soldier to steal. A soldier must be honest, honorable, and brave. But if he robs his own comrades, there's no honor in him—he's scum. Go on! Go on!"
And so the swishing of the switches continued, along with the desperate but unnatural screams.
"Go on, go on!" said the major.
A young officer with a bewildered, pained look on his face stepped away from the scene and glanced questioningly at Prince Andrew as he rode past.

Prince Andrew, having reached the front line, rode along it. On the right and left flanks, the Russian and French positions were far apart, but in the center—where the men carrying the flag of truce had passed that morning—the lines were so close that soldiers on each side could see one another's faces and call out to each other. Besides the soldiers forming the picket line on both sides, there were plenty of curious onlookers who stood there joking, laughing, and staring at their strange foreign enemies.

Since early morning, despite strict orders not to approach the picket line, the officers hadn't been able to keep the gawkers away. The soldiers on picket duty, like showmen displaying an oddity, had stopped paying attention to the French and were focused instead on the spectators. They looked bored, waiting to be relieved. Prince Andrew halted to observe the French.

"Look! Look at that!" one soldier was saying to another, pointing at a Russian musketeer who had walked right up to the picket line with an officer and was talking rapidly and excitedly to a French grenadier. "Listen to him jabber away! Not bad, eh? The Frenchman can barely keep up. Go on, Sidorov!"
"Wait, just listen. He's brilliant!" answered Sidorov, who was considered an expert in French.

The soldier they were all laughing about was Dolokhov. Prince Andrew recognized him and stopped to listen. Dolokhov had come over from the left flank, where his regiment was posted, along with his captain.
"Go on, go on! Keep going!" the officer urged, leaning forward, trying not to miss a word of a conversation he couldn't understand. "More, please—more! What's he saying?"

Dolokhov didn't answer the captain. He'd been drawn into a heated argument with the French grenadier. Naturally, they were talking about the campaign. The Frenchman, confusing the Austrians with the Russians, was trying to claim that the Russians had surrendered and fled all the way from Ulm. Dolokhov insisted that the Russians hadn't surrendered at all—that they'd beaten the French.
"We have orders to drive you out of here, and drive you out we will," said Dolokhov.
"Just make sure you and your Cossacks don't get captured!" the French grenadier shot back.
The French onlookers laughed.
"We'll make you dance the way we did under Suvorov," said Dolokhov.
* "On vous fera danser."
"What's he going on about?" asked one of the Frenchmen.
* "What's he singing about?"
"Ancient history," said another, guessing it referred to a previous war. "The Emperor will teach your Suvorov just as he's taught everyone else."
"Bonaparte—" Dolokhov began, but the Frenchman cut him off.
"Not Bonaparte! He is the Emperor! Good God!" the man cried angrily.
"The devil take your Emperor!"
And Dolokhov cursed at him in rough soldier's Russian, shouldered his musket, and walked away.
"Let's go, Ivan Lukich," he said to the captain.
"Now that's how you speak French!" said the picket soldiers. "Come on, Sidorov—your turn!"

Sidorov turned to the French, gave a wink, and launched into a stream of rapid, meaningless sounds: "Kari, mala, tafa, safi, muter, Kaska!" he said, trying to give his nonsense an expressive, dramatic tone.

"Ho! ho! ho! Ha! ha! ha! ha! Ooh! ooh!" Peals of such healthy, good-natured laughter burst from the soldiers that it crossed the lines and infected the French too, so completely that it seemed like the only sensible thing to do would be to unload the muskets, dump the ammunition, and everyone go home.
But the guns stayed loaded, the loopholes in the blockhouses and trenches gaped just as menacingly, and the unlimbered cannons still faced each other, exactly as before.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: Having ridden along the entire line from right flank to left, Prince Andrew made his way up to the battery from which the staff officer had told him the whole field was visible. He dismounted and stopped beside the farthest of the four unlimbered cannons. An artillery sentry was pacing back and forth in front of the guns; he snapped to attention when the officer appeared but, at a gesture, resumed his steady, monotonous march. Behind the guns stood their limbers, and further back, picket ropes and the artillerymen's campfires. Off to the left, not far from the last cannon, was a small, newly built wattle hut from which came the sound of officers talking animatedly.

It was true that from this battery you could see nearly the entire Russian position and most of the enemy's as well. Directly ahead, on the crest of the opposite hill, lay the village of Schon Grabern, and to the left and right in three places the French troops were visible amid the smoke of their campfires—most of them evidently in the village itself and behind the hill. To the left of the village, through the smoke, something that looked like a battery could be made out, though it was impossible to see clearly with the naked eye. The Russian right flank was positioned on a fairly steep slope that overlooked the French. The infantry was stationed there, and at the far end, the dragoons. In the center, where Tushin's battery stood and where Prince Andrew was now surveying the position, was the most direct and gradual descent to the stream that separated the two armies. On the left, Russian troops were close to a wooded area where bonfires smoked as infantry soldiers felled trees. The French line was wider than the Russian one, and it was obvious they could easily outflank both sides. Behind the Russian position was a steep, deep ravine that would make it very difficult for artillery and cavalry to retreat. Prince Andrew took out his notebook and, leaning against a cannon, sketched a plan of the position. He jotted down notes on two points he intended to raise with Bagration. His idea was, first, to concentrate all the artillery in the center, and second, to pull the cavalry back behind the ravine. Prince Andrew, who was always close to the commander in chief, who followed large-scale troop movements and general strategy closely, and who constantly studied historical accounts of battles, instinctively envisioned the coming engagement in broad strokes. He imagined only the key scenarios: "If the enemy attacks the right flank," he told himself, "the Kiev grenadiers and the Podolsk chasseurs must hold their ground until reserves arrive from the center. In that case, the dragoons could launch a successful flanking counterattack. If they attack our center, we place the center battery on this high ground, pull the left flank back under its cover, and retreat toward the ravine in echelons." So he reasoned... The whole time he'd been standing by the gun, he'd heard the officers' voices clearly from the hut, but as often happens, hadn't really been listening. Suddenly, though, one voice caught his attention—its tone was so genuine that he couldn't help but listen.

"No, my friend," said a pleasant voice that seemed somehow familiar to Prince Andrew, "what I'm saying is that if we could know what lies beyond death, none of us would be afraid of it. That's the truth, my friend."
A younger voice broke in: "Afraid or not, there's no escaping it either way."

"Still, people are afraid! You clever types," said a third, deeper voice, interrupting both of them. "Of course you artillery men have it good—you can bring everything along with you: vodka, snacks, the works."
The owner of this hearty voice, clearly an infantry officer, laughed.

"Yes, people are afraid," continued the first speaker, the one with the familiar voice. "They're afraid of the unknown—that's what it comes down to. We can talk all we want about the soul rising up to heaven... but we know perfectly well there is no heaven—just atmosphere."
The deep voice interrupted the artillery officer again.
"Come on, pour us some of that herb vodka of yours, Tushin," it said.
"Why, that's the captain who was standing in the sutler's tent without his boots!" thought Prince Andrew. He recognized the agreeable, philosophizing voice with pleasure.
"Herb vodka? Of course!" said Tushin. "But still, to think about what comes after..."

He never finished. At that moment there was a whistle in the air—closer and closer, faster and louder, louder and faster—and a cannonball, as though it hadn't quite finished making its point, slammed into the earth near the hut with inhuman force, sending up a fountain of dirt. The ground seemed to groan from the terrible impact.

And instantly Tushin, his short pipe still clenched in the corner of his mouth and his kind, intelligent face gone noticeably pale, came rushing out of the hut, followed by the owner of the hearty voice—a dashing infantry officer who hurried off toward his company, buttoning his coat as he ran.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: Remounting his horse, Prince Andrew lingered by the battery, watching the puff of smoke from the gun that had fired the shot. His eyes swept rapidly across the broad field, and he could see that the previously motionless French masses had begun to stir, and that there really was a battery on their left. The smoke from it hadn't yet cleared before another puff appeared, followed by the boom of a cannon. The battle had begun. Prince Andrew wheeled his horse around and galloped back to Grunth to find Prince Bagration. Behind him, the cannonade was growing louder and more frequent. Clearly, the Russian guns had started firing back. From the low ground where the parley had taken place that morning came the crackle of musket fire.

Lemarrois had just arrived at a gallop bearing Bonaparte's harsh letter, and Murat, humiliated and desperate to make up for his blunder, had immediately sent his forces forward to attack the center and outflank both Russian wings, hoping to crush this pitiful detachment before evening, before the Emperor himself could arrive.
"It's started. Here it is!" thought Prince Andrew, feeling the blood rush to his heart. "But where—and how—will I find my Toulon?"

Riding past the companies that had been eating porridge and drinking vodka just fifteen minutes ago, he saw the same scene everywhere: soldiers rapidly forming ranks, readying their muskets, and on every face the same fierce eagerness that burned in his own heart. "It's started! Here it is—terrifying but thrilling!" That was what each soldier's and each officer's face seemed to say.

Before he reached the earthworks being thrown up, he saw, in the dull light of the autumn evening, mounted men riding toward him. The one in front, wearing a Cossack cloak and a lambskin cap on a white horse, was Prince Bagration. Prince Andrew pulled up and waited; Bagration reined in his horse, recognized Prince Andrew, and gave him a nod. He kept looking straight ahead while Prince Andrew reported what he had observed.

The feeling—"It's started! Here it is!"—was visible even on Prince Bagration's hard, dark face with its half-shut, sleepy eyes. Prince Andrew studied that impassive face with anxious curiosity, wanting to know what, if anything, this man was thinking and feeling at that moment. "Is there actually anything behind that expressionless mask?" Prince Andrew wondered. Bagration inclined his head to signal agreement with what Prince Andrew told him and said, "Very good," in a tone suggesting that everything happening was exactly what he'd expected. Prince Andrew, out of breath from his hard ride, spoke quickly. Bagration, pronouncing his words with an Eastern accent, spoke especially slowly, as though to demonstrate that there was no need for haste. Still, he set his horse to a trot toward Tushin's battery. Prince Andrew followed with the rest of the staff. Behind Bagration rode a staff officer, the prince's personal adjutant, Zherkov, an orderly officer, the duty staff officer on a handsome bob-tailed horse, and a civilian—an accountant who had asked permission to observe the battle out of curiosity. The accountant, a stout man with a round face, looked around with a naive smile of delight and cut a strange figure among the hussars, Cossacks, and adjutants, bouncing along in his wool coat on a horse fitted with a convoy officer's saddle.
"He wants to see a battle," Zherkov said to Bolkonsky, nodding toward the accountant. "But he's already got a stomachache."
"Oh, stop it!" said the accountant with a beaming but slightly sly smile, flattered to be the butt of Zherkov's joke and deliberately playing up his own foolishness.
"It is very strange, mon Monsieur Prince," said the staff officer. (He remembered there was some special way to address a prince in French, but couldn't quite get it right.)
By now they were all approaching Tushin's battery, and a cannonball struck the ground in front of them.
"What was that that fell?" asked the accountant with a guileless smile.
"A French pancake," Zherkov replied.
"So that's what they fire at you? How frightening!" said the accountant.

He seemed to swell with satisfaction. He'd barely finished speaking when they heard another unexpectedly violent whistling that suddenly ended with a thud into something soft—f-f-flop!—and a Cossack riding slightly to the right and behind the accountant crashed to the earth along with his horse. Zherkov and the staff officer ducked over their saddles and yanked their horses aside. The accountant stopped, staring at the fallen Cossack with wide-eyed curiosity. The Cossack was dead, but the horse still thrashed.

Prince Bagration squinted, glanced around, and, seeing what had caused the commotion, turned away with indifference, as if to say, "Is this really worth stopping for?" He reined in his horse with the skill of an expert rider and, bending slightly, freed his saber, which had caught in his cloak. It was an old-fashioned saber, not the kind in common use anymore. Prince Andrew remembered the story of how Suvorov had given his saber to Bagration in Italy, and the memory felt especially right at that moment. They had reached the battery where Prince Andrew had stood earlier surveying the field.
"Whose company?" Prince Bagration asked an artilleryman standing by an ammunition wagon.
He asked, "Whose company?" but what he really meant was, "You're not scared up here, are you?" And the artilleryman understood perfectly.
"Captain Tushin's, your excellency!" shouted a red-haired, freckled gunner in a cheerful voice, standing at attention.
"Right, right," Bagration muttered, as if turning something over in his mind, and rode past the limbers to the farthest cannon.

As he approached, a deafening blast erupted from it, and in the sudden cloud of smoke that enveloped the gun, they could see the crew straining to roll it quickly back into position. A huge, broad-shouldered gunner—Number One—stood with legs wide apart, gripping a sponge-staff, and sprang to the wheel. Number Two, his hands trembling, rammed a charge into the cannon's mouth. Captain Tushin, short and round-shouldered, stumbled over the tail of the gun carriage as he came forward and, not noticing the general, shaded his eyes with his small hand and peered out at the enemy.
"Elevate two lines more and it'll be perfect," he called out in his thin voice, trying to sound bold—a tone that didn't suit his slight frame at all. "Number Two! Fire, Medvedev!"

Bagration called to him, and Tushin, raising three fingers to his cap in a bashful, awkward gesture—less like a military salute than a priest's blessing—approached the general. Although Tushin's guns were supposed to be covering the valley, he had been lobbing incendiary shells at the village of Schon Grabern, which lay directly ahead, where large masses of French troops were advancing.

No one had given Tushin specific orders about where to aim, but after consulting his sergeant major Zakharchenko, whom he deeply respected, he'd decided on his own that setting the village on fire would be useful. "Very good!" said Bagration in response to the officer's report, and began carefully surveying the entire battlefield spread before him. The French had pushed closest on the right. Below the heights where the Kiev regiment was stationed, in the hollow where the stream flowed, came the stirring, rolling crackle of musket fire. And much further to the right, beyond the dragoons, a staff officer pointed out to Bagration a French column that was moving to outflank them. To the left, the horizon was bounded by the nearby woods. Prince Bagration ordered two battalions from the center sent to reinforce the right flank. The staff officer dared to point out that if those battalions left, the guns would be completely unprotected. Bagration turned to the officer and stared at him in silence with his dull eyes. Prince Andrew felt the officer's concern was perfectly justified, and that there really was no good answer to it. But at that moment an adjutant came galloping up with a message from the colonel commanding the troops in the hollow: massive French forces were bearing down on them, and his regiment was falling apart, retreating toward the Kiev grenadiers. Prince Bagration gave a nod of acknowledgment. He rode off to the right at a walk and sent an adjutant to the dragoons with orders to attack the French. But this adjutant returned half an hour later with the news that the dragoon commander had already pulled back behind the ravine—heavy fire had been concentrated on his position and he was losing men for nothing—so he'd pushed some sharpshooters into the woods instead.
"Very good!" said Bagration.

As he rode away from the battery, firing broke out on the left too. Since it was too far for him to reach the left flank in time, Bagration sent Zherkov to tell the general in command there—the same one who had paraded his regiment before Kutuzov at Braunau—to pull back as fast as possible behind the hollow to the rear, since the right flank probably couldn't hold the enemy's assault much longer. As for Tushin and the battalion supporting his battery, they were completely forgotten. Prince Andrew listened closely to Bagration's exchanges with the various officers and the orders he issued, and to his surprise realized that no real orders were being given at all. What Bagration actually did was try to make it appear that everything happening—whether by necessity, by chance, or by the initiative of subordinate commanders—was being done, if not by his direct command, then at least in keeping with his intentions. Prince Andrew noticed, though, that despite the fact that events unfolded independently of Bagration's will, the man's tact made his presence genuinely valuable. Officers who approached him with worried faces became calm; soldiers and officers greeted him warmly, visibly perked up around him, and clearly wanted to show their bravery in front of him.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: Having reached the highest point of the right flank, Prince Bagration began riding downhill toward the sound of gunfire, though the smoke made it impossible to see anything. The closer they got to the hollow, the less they could see but the more intensely they felt the proximity of the actual fighting. They started meeting wounded men. One, his head bleeding and his cap gone, was being dragged along by two soldiers gripping him under the arms. He was gurgling and spitting blood—a bullet had clearly struck him in the mouth or throat. Another walked along steadily under his own power, but without his musket, groaning loudly and swinging his arm, which had just been wounded. Blood streamed from it down over his greatcoat as from an uncorked bottle. He'd only just been hit, and his face showed more fear than pain. Crossing a road, they descended a steep slope and saw several men lying on the ground; they also encountered a crowd of soldiers, some unwounded. The soldiers were climbing the hill, breathing hard, and despite the general's presence, they were talking loudly and waving their arms. Up ahead, through the smoke, rows of gray cloaks were already visible, and an officer who spotted Bagration ran shouting after the retreating soldiers, trying to order them back. Bagration rode up to the line, along which gunfire crackled first here, then there, drowning out voices and shouted commands. The air was thick with smoke. The soldiers' excited faces were blackened with it. Some were ramming charges, others pouring powder into touchpans or pulling cartridges from their pouches, still others were firing—though through the drifting, windless smoke, who they were firing at was impossible to tell. A pleasant humming and whistling of bullets filled the air. "What's going on here?" thought Prince Andrew as he approached the crowd. "It can't be an attack—they aren't moving. It can't be a square—they aren't formed up for that."

The regimental commander, a thin, frail-looking old man with a kind smile—his drooping eyelids covering more than half his eyes and giving him a gentle expression—rode up to Bagration and greeted him like a host welcoming an honored guest. He reported that his regiment had been attacked by French cavalry, and that although the attack had been repulsed, he'd lost more than half his men. He used the military term "repulsed" to describe what had happened, but in truth he himself had no idea what had actually occurred during that half hour. All he really knew was that at the start of the action, shells and bullets had begun flying all over his regiment, hitting his men. Then someone had shouted "Cavalry!" and his soldiers had started shooting. They were still shooting now—not at the cavalry, which had vanished, but at French infantry that had moved into the hollow and was firing at them. Prince Bagration nodded, as though this was precisely what he'd expected. Turning to his adjutant, he ordered him to bring down the two battalions of the Sixth Chasseurs they'd just passed. Prince Andrew was struck by the change in Bagration's expression at that moment. His face now showed the focused, joyful determination you see in a man who, on a sweltering day, takes one final running start before plunging into the water. The dull, sleepy look was gone, and so was the pretense of deep deliberation. His round, steady, hawklike eyes stared ahead with eager, almost disdainful intensity, fixing on nothing in particular, though his movements remained slow and measured.

The regimental commander pleaded with Bagration to go back, insisting it was too dangerous where they stood. "Please, your excellency, for God's sake!" he kept saying, glancing at a staff officer for support—but the staff officer looked away. "There—do you see?" He gestured at the bullets that whistled, sang, and hissed past them constantly. He spoke in the imploring tone a carpenter uses with a gentleman who has picked up an axe: "We're used to this sort of thing, but you, sir, will blister your hands." He spoke as if the bullets couldn't possibly kill him, and his half-shut eyes gave his words even more persuasive force. The staff officer added his pleas to the colonel's, but Bagration didn't respond. He simply ordered the troops to stop firing and re-form to make room for the two approaching battalions. As he spoke, the curtain of smoke hiding the hollow was swept from right to left by a rising breeze, as if pulled by an invisible hand, and the opposite hill—with French soldiers moving about on it—was suddenly revealed. Every eye locked instinctively on the French column advancing toward them, winding down over the broken ground. You could already make out the soldiers' shaggy caps, tell the officers from the enlisted men, and see the regimental standard flapping against its staff.
"They march beautifully," someone in Bagration's group remarked.
The head of the French column had already descended into the hollow. The collision would happen on this side of it...

The remnants of the regiment that had been engaged quickly reformed and shifted to the right. From behind them, sweeping aside the stragglers, came two battalions of the Sixth Chasseurs in excellent order. Before they'd even reached Bagration, the heavy, rhythmic tread of massed men marching in step could be heard. On their left flank, nearest to Bagration, marched a company commander—a round-faced, handsome man with a stupid, blissful expression: the same officer who had rushed out of the wattle hut earlier. At that moment, he was clearly thinking about nothing except how magnificent he would look as he passed the commander.

With the self-assurance of a man on parade, he stepped lightly on his muscular legs as if gliding, stretching to his full height effortlessly, his ease a stark contrast to the heavy tramp of the soldiers keeping pace beside him. He carried a narrow, unsheathed sword close against his leg—small, curved, not really a weapon at all—and kept glancing now at the senior officers, now back at his men, all without breaking stride, his whole powerful body pivoting fluidly. It was as if every fiber of his being were focused on looking perfect as he passed the commander, and since he felt he was succeeding, he was perfectly happy. "Left... left... left..." he seemed to repeat to himself with each step, and in time to this rhythm, with stern but varied expressions, the wall of soldiers burdened with packs and muskets marched forward, each one seeming to repeat that same silent cadence: "Left... left... left..." A portly major skirted a bush, puffing and losing the beat. A soldier who'd fallen behind, alarm on his face at his own transgression, trotted to catch up. A cannonball sliced through the air over the heads of Bagration and his suite and slammed into the column, right in the rhythm of "Left... left!" "Close up!" rang out the company commander's voice, jaunty as ever. The soldiers curved around the spot where the ball had struck, and an old noncommissioned officer on the flank, who had stopped beside the fallen men, ran to catch up with his line. With a little hop he fell back into step, glanced back angrily, and through the ominous silence, beneath the regular tramp of boots striking the ground in unison, you could almost hear it still: left... left... left...
"Well done, lads!" said Prince Bagration.

"Glad to serve, your ex-len-cy!" came back a ragged shout from the ranks. One grim-faced soldier on the left flank turned his eyes toward Bagration as he shouted, his expression seeming to say: "We know that ourselves!" Another, not daring to look around for fear of losing focus, shouted with his mouth stretched wide and marched on.
The order came to halt and drop packs.

Bagration rode along the ranks that had just marched past and dismounted. He handed his reins to a Cossack, took off his felt cloak and passed it over, stretched his legs, and straightened his cap. The head of the French column, officers in the lead, appeared from below the hill.

"Forward, with God!" said Bagration in a resolute, ringing voice. He turned briefly to face the front line and, swinging his arms slightly, began walking forward over the rough ground with the awkward, rolling gait of a cavalryman. Prince Andrew felt an invisible force drawing him forward, and a surge of happiness swept through him.

The French were already close. Walking beside Bagration, Prince Andrew could clearly make out their bandoliers, red epaulets, even their faces. He distinctly saw an old French officer with gaitered legs and feet turned out, struggling up the hill. Prince Bagration gave no more orders and walked silently on ahead of the ranks. Then, all at once, a volley of shots erupted from the French side—smoke appeared along their ragged line—and musket fire crackled. Several Russian soldiers fell, among them the round-faced officer who had marched so cheerfully, so proudly. But at the very instant the first shot rang out, Bagration looked back and shouted, "Hurrah!"

"Hurrah-ah-ah!" A long, drawn-out roar rose from the Russian ranks, and the men surged past Bagration—racing each other, an irregular but joyful, eager crowd—charging down the hill toward the disordered enemy.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: The attack by the Sixth Chasseurs secured the retreat of the right flank. In the center, Tushin's forgotten battery—which had managed to set fire to the village of Schon Grabern—held up the French advance. The French were busy putting out the fire, which the wind kept spreading, and that bought the Russians time to pull back. The retreat of the center behind the ravine was rushed and noisy, but at least the different companies didn't get jumbled together. The left flank, however—made up of the Azov and Podolsk infantry regiments and the Pavlograd hussars—was simultaneously attacked and outflanked by superior French forces under Lannes and thrown into chaos. Bagration had sent Zherkov to the general commanding the left flank with orders to retreat immediately.

Zherkov, keeping his hand at his cap, wheeled his horse around and galloped off. But the moment he left Bagration's side, his nerve failed him. Panic seized him, and he simply could not go where it was dangerous.

When he reached the left flank, instead of riding to the front where the firing was, he went looking for the general and his staff in places where they couldn't possibly be. And so the order was never delivered.

Command of the left flank belonged by seniority to the colonel of the regiment Kutuzov had reviewed at Braunau—the one where Dolokhov was serving as a private. But command of the extreme left had been given to the colonel of the Pavlograd hussars, Rostov's regiment, and a bitter misunderstanding erupted between the two commanders. They were thoroughly infuriated with each other and, long after the fighting had begun on the right and the French were already advancing, they were still locked in a quarrel whose only real purpose was to insult one another. Meanwhile, their regiments—cavalry and infantry alike—were completely unprepared for battle. From privates to generals, nobody was expecting a fight. They were all engaged in peaceful activities: the cavalry feeding their horses, the infantry gathering firewood.

"He is higher in rank zan I am," said the German colonel of the hussars, his face flushing, to an adjutant who had ridden up. "So let him do vhat he vill, but I cannot sacrifice my hussars. Bugler, sound ze retreat!"

But there was no more time to waste. Cannon and musket fire, blending together, thundered on the right and in the center, while the long coats of Lannes's sharpshooters were already visible crossing the mill dam and forming up within twice a musket shot's range. The infantry general walked over to his horse with jerky steps, mounted up, drew himself very straight and tall, and rode over to the Pavlograd colonel. The two commanders met with polite bows, barely concealing the hostility in their hearts.
"Once again, Colonel," said the general, "I cannot leave half my men behind in the woods. I'm asking you—I'm begging you—to take up your position and prepare to attack."
"And I am begging you not to interfere in vhat is not your affair!" the colonel suddenly snapped. "If you vere cavalry..."
"I am not cavalry, Colonel, but I am a Russian general, and if you don't know that..."

"I know it perfectly vell, your excellency!" the colonel suddenly shouted, spurring his horse forward, his face going purple. "Vill you be so kind as to come to ze front and see for yourself zat zis position is no good? I vill not destroy my men for your pleasure!"
"You forget yourself, Colonel! I am not considering my own pleasure, and I won't have anyone say that I am!"

Taking the colonel's outburst as a challenge to his courage, the general puffed out his chest and rode beside him toward the front line, scowling, as if the dispute could be settled right there among the flying bullets. They reached the line, several rounds whizzed past them, and they stopped in silence. There was nothing new to see from there—it had already been obvious from further back that cavalry couldn't operate among the bushes and broken terrain, and that the French were outflanking the left. The general and the colonel stared at each other sternly and significantly, like two fighting cocks before a match, each trying to detect signs of cowardice in the other. Both passed the test. Since there was nothing to say, and neither man wanted to be the first to leave the zone of fire and give the other grounds to accuse him, they might have stood there indefinitely, testing each other's nerve—had they not heard, just then, the rattle of musket fire and muffled shouting almost behind them, in the woods. The French had attacked the men gathering firewood in the copse. It was no longer possible for the hussars to retreat with the infantry. They were cut off from their line of retreat on the left by the French. However bad the position was, the only option now was to attack—to cut a way through.

Rostov's squadron barely had time to mount before it was halted, facing the enemy. Once again, as at the bridge over the Enns, there was nothing between the squadron and the enemy, and once again that terrible, invisible line of uncertainty and fear—the line between the living and the dead—lay between them. Everyone felt it, and the question of whether they would cross it, and how, filled them all with dread.

The colonel rode to the front, angrily snapped at the officers' questions, and—like a man desperately determined to have his way—gave an order. Nobody said anything specific, but the rumor of an attack rippled through the squadron. The command to form up rang out. Sabers whistled as they slid from their scabbards. Still, no one moved. The troops on the left flank, hussars and infantry alike, could sense that their commander didn't know what to do himself, and his uncertainty spread to every man.
"If only they'd hurry!" thought Rostov, feeling that the moment had finally come for the kind of glorious charge he'd heard his fellow hussars describe so many times.
"Fo'ward, with God, lads!" rang out Denisov's voice. "At a t-wot, fo'ward!"
The horses' hindquarters began to sway in the front rank. Rook tugged at his reins and broke into motion on his own.

To his right, ahead of him, Rostov could see the front line of his hussars and, further off, a dark line he couldn't quite make out but assumed was the enemy. Shots were audible, though still some distance away.
"Faster!" came the command, and Rostov felt Rook's flanks drop as the horse broke into a gallop.

Rostov anticipated his horse's every movement and felt more exhilarated by the second. He'd fixed his eyes on a lone tree ahead. That tree had been in the middle of the line that had seemed so terrifying—and now he'd crossed it, and not only was there nothing terrible, but everything was becoming more thrilling, more alive. "Oh, how I'll cut at him!" thought Rostov, gripping the hilt of his saber.

"Hurrah!" roared the voices around him. "Just let someone come at me now," thought Rostov, driving his spurs into Rook and urging him to a full gallop until he outpaced the rest. The enemy was visible ahead. Then suddenly something like a birch broom seemed to sweep across the squadron. Rostov raised his saber to strike—but at that instant the trooper Nikitenko, who'd been galloping just ahead, shot away from him, and Rostov felt, as in a dream, that he was being carried forward at an impossible speed yet somehow staying in the same spot. Behind him, Bondarchuk, a hussar he knew, crashed into him and glared angrily. Bondarchuk's horse swerved and galloped past.

"Why aren't I moving? I've fallen. I'm killed!" Rostov asked himself and answered in the same breath. He was alone in the middle of a field. Instead of galloping horses and hussars' backs, all he could see was the motionless earth and stubble around him. Something warm and wet spread under his arm. "No—I'm wounded, and the horse is killed." Rook tried to push himself up on his front legs but fell back, pinning his rider's leg. Blood poured from the horse's head; he thrashed but couldn't stand. Rostov tried to rise too but fell back—his sabretache had gotten tangled in the saddle. Where the Russians were, where the French were, he had no idea. There was nobody near.

Having freed his leg, he stood up. "Where is the line now—that line that had so sharply divided the two armies?" he asked himself, and couldn't answer. "Has something terrible happened to me?" he wondered as he got to his feet. At that moment he felt something extra hanging from his numb left arm. His wrist felt like it belonged to someone else. He examined his hand carefully, searching in vain for blood. "Ah, here come some people," he thought with a rush of joy, seeing men running toward him. "They'll help me!" The first man wore a strange-looking shako and a blue cloak; he was swarthy, sunburned, with a hooked nose. Then came two more, and many more behind them. One of them said something in a language that wasn't Russian. Among the men at the back, wearing the same unfamiliar shakos, was a Russian hussar being held by the arms, his horse led behind him.

"It must be one of ours—a prisoner. Wait... Could they actually take me prisoner too? Who are these men?" thought Rostov, barely believing his eyes. "Can they be French?" He stared at the approaching Frenchmen, and though just a moment before he'd been galloping straight at them with every intention of hacking them to pieces, their nearness now felt so horrifying that he couldn't trust his own eyes. "Who are they? Why are they running? Can they be coming for me? And why? To kill me? Me—whom everyone loves?" He thought of his mother's love, his family's love, his friends' love, and the idea that these strangers wanted to kill him seemed impossible. "But maybe they actually will." For more than ten seconds he stood rooted to the spot, unable to comprehend what was happening. The first Frenchman, the hook-nosed one, was now so close that Rostov could read the expression on his face. And the sight of that excited, foreign face—the man's bayonet lowered, holding his breath, running so lightly—terrified Rostov. He grabbed his pistol and, instead of firing it, hurled it at the Frenchman and ran for the bushes with everything he had. He no longer ran with the doubt and inner conflict he'd felt crossing the bridge at Enns. He ran with the instinct of a hare fleeing hounds. One single feeling possessed him completely: fear for his young, happy life. Bounding over furrows, he sprinted across the field with the same desperate speed he'd once shown playing tag, turning now and then to glance back with his kind, pale, young face. A shudder of terror ran through him: "No, don't look back," he thought, but when he reached the bushes he looked around one more time. The French had fallen behind, and just as he turned, the first man slowed from a run to a walk, turned, and shouted something to a comrade further back. Rostov stopped. "No, this is some kind of mistake," he thought. "They can't really want to kill me." But at the same time his left arm felt as if a seventy-pound weight were tied to it. He couldn't run anymore. The Frenchman stopped too and took aim. Rostov squeezed his eyes shut and ducked. One bullet, then another, whistled past him. He gathered his last remaining strength, grabbed his left hand with his right, and reached the bushes. Behind them were Russian sharpshooters.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: The infantry regiments that had been caught off guard at the edge of the woods came pouring out of the trees, companies jumbled together, retreating as a disorganized mob. One soldier, in his terror, let out the senseless cry "Cut off!"—those words that are so devastating in battle—and that single shout infected the entire crowd with panic.
"Surrounded! Cut off! We're done for!" screamed the men as they fled.

The instant he heard the gunfire and the shouts behind him, the general realized something terrible had happened to his regiment. The thought that he—a model officer with decades of unblemished service—might be held responsible at headquarters for negligence or incompetence hit him so hard that he forgot about the obstinate cavalry colonel, forgot his own dignity as a general, and above all forgot any concern for his personal safety. He grabbed the back of his saddle, spurred his horse, and galloped toward his regiment through a storm of bullets that flew all around him but, by some miracle, missed. His one desire was to find out what had happened and, at any cost, fix whatever had gone wrong—so that he, a model officer of twenty-two years' service who had never once been reprimanded, would not be blamed.

Having galloped safely through the French lines, he reached a field behind the copse, across which his men were streaming in all directions, running downhill in defiance of every order. The decisive moment of moral crisis—the kind that determines the outcome of battles—had arrived. Would this panicked mob of soldiers respond to their commander's voice, or would they ignore him and keep running? Despite his desperate shouting—the kind that used to terrify his soldiers—despite his furious, purple face, distorted beyond recognition, despite the wild flourishing of his saber, the soldiers kept running, talking, firing into the air, and refusing to obey. The moral crisis was tipping unmistakably toward a rout.

The general had a coughing fit from all the shouting and the powder smoke and stopped in despair. Everything seemed lost. But at that moment, the attacking French suddenly and inexplicably turned and ran back, disappearing from the edge of the woods. Russian sharpshooters appeared in the copse. It was Timokhin's company—the only unit that had held together in the forest. They'd been lying in ambush in a ditch and now burst upon the French from behind. Timokhin, armed with nothing but a sword, had charged the enemy with such a wild cry and such furious, almost crazed determination that the stunned French had dropped their muskets and fled. Dolokhov, running alongside Timokhin, killed a Frenchman at point-blank range and was the first to seize a surrendering French officer by the collar. The Russian fugitives turned around. The battalions reformed. The French, who had come within an inch of splitting the left flank in two, were beaten back for the moment. The reserve units linked up again, and the fighting came to an end. The regimental commander and Major Ekonomov had halted by a bridge to let the retreating companies file past when a soldier walked up and grabbed the commander's stirrup, practically leaning against him. The man wore a bluish broadcloth coat, had no pack or cap, his head was bandaged, and a French ammunition pouch hung from his shoulder. He held an officer's sword in his hand. The soldier was pale, his blue eyes stared insolently into the commander's face, and his lips were set in a smile. Though the commander was busy giving instructions to Major Ekonomov, he couldn't help noticing the man.

"Your excellency, two trophies," said Dolokhov, pointing to the French sword and pouch. "I took an officer prisoner. I stopped the company from retreating." He was breathing hard from exhaustion and spoke in short, clipped sentences. "The entire company can confirm it. Please remember this, your excellency."
"All right, all right," the commander replied, and turned back to Major Ekonomov.
But Dolokhov didn't leave. He untied the handkerchief around his head, pulled it off, and showed the blood matted in his hair.
"A bayonet wound. I stayed at the front. Remember, your excellency."

Tushin's battery had been entirely forgotten, and only at the very end of the battle did Prince Bagration, still hearing cannon fire from the center, send his orderly staff officer—and later Prince Andrew as well—to order the battery to pull back as quickly as possible. When the infantry support assigned to Tushin's battery had been moved away mid-battle by someone's order, the battery had simply kept firing. The only reason it wasn't overrun by the French was that the enemy couldn't imagine anyone would have the audacity to keep firing from four completely undefended guns. On the contrary, the sheer aggressiveness of this battery led the French to believe that the main Russian forces were concentrated here, in the center. Twice they'd tried to storm the position, and both times they'd been driven back by grapeshot from four lonely guns on the hilltop.
Shortly after Bagration had left, Tushin managed to set fire to Schon Grabern.
"Look at them scramble! It's burning! Look at the smoke! Magnificent! Look at the smoke, the smoke!" the artillerymen exclaimed, their spirits soaring.

All the guns, without waiting for orders, opened fire toward the blaze. Egging each other on, the soldiers shouted with every shot: "Beautiful! That's the stuff! Look at that! Magnificent!" The fire, fanned by the breeze, was spreading fast. The French columns that had advanced past the village fell back. But as if in retaliation, the enemy brought up ten guns to the right of the village and began shelling Tushin's battery.

In their childlike excitement over the fire and their success in bombarding the French, the artillerymen didn't even notice this new battery until two balls, and then four more, crashed among their guns—one toppling two horses and another ripping off a wagon driver's leg. But their high spirits weren't dampened, only redirected. The dead horses were replaced from a reserve gun carriage, the wounded were carried away, and all four guns were turned against the ten-gun battery. Tushin's fellow officer had been killed at the start of the engagement, and within an hour seventeen of the forty men in the gun crews had been put out of action. But the artillerymen were as spirited and lively as ever. Twice they spotted French infantry approaching from below and blasted them with grapeshot.

Little Tushin, moving about weakly and awkwardly, kept telling his orderly, "Refill my pipe for that one!" and then, scattering sparks, ran forward shielding his eyes with his small hand to peer at the French.
"Give it to 'em, lads!" he kept saying, grabbing the gun wheels himself and working the elevation screws.

Through the smoke, deafened by the constant explosions that made him flinch every time, Tushin ran from gun to gun without ever taking his pipe from his mouth—now aiming, now counting charges, now shouting orders about replacing dead or wounded horses and hitching fresh ones, calling out in his thin, high-pitched, wavering voice. His face grew more and more animated. Only when a man was killed or wounded did he wince and turn away from the sight, shouting angrily at the soldiers who, as always happens, hesitated about carrying off the dead and injured. The soldiers—mostly big, handsome men, as is typical in artillery companies, a head taller and twice as broad as their little officer—watched their commander the way children watch a grown-up in an awkward situation. Whatever expression crossed his face was instantly mirrored on theirs.

Thanks to the overwhelming noise and the demands of constant action, Tushin felt not the slightest trace of fear. The thought that he might be killed or badly wounded never once entered his mind. On the contrary, he grew more and more exhilarated. It felt to him as though an enormously long time had passed—nearly a full day—since he'd first spotted the enemy and fired that opening shot, and that the patch of ground he was standing on was a place he'd known for years. Although he was thinking of everything, weighing everything, doing everything that the best officer in his situation could possibly do, he was in a state closer to feverish delirium or intoxication.

From the deafening roar of his own guns around him, the whistle and thud of enemy cannonballs, the flushed and sweating faces of his crew bustling around the guns, the sight of blood—human and horse—the small puffs of smoke on the enemy's hill (each one followed inevitably by a ball that flew past and struck the ground, a man, a gun, a horse)—from all of this, a fantastical world of his own making had taken hold of his mind and was, at that moment, giving him pleasure. The enemy's cannon were not guns in his imagination but pipes, from which an invisible smoker occasionally blew puffs of smoke.
"There... he's puffing again," Tushin muttered to himself as a small cloud rose from the hill and drifted in a streak to the left on the wind.
"Now watch for the ball... we'll toss it right back."
"What did you say, your honor?" asked an artilleryman standing close by, who'd heard him muttering.
"Nothing... just a shell," he answered.

"Come on, Matvevna old girl!" he said to himself. "Matvevna" was the pet name his imagination had given to the farthest gun in the battery—a large, old-fashioned piece. The French swarming around their guns looked to him like ants. In this fantasy world of his, the handsome drunk who was Number One on the second gun's crew had become "uncle"; Tushin watched him more than anyone else and took delight in his every movement. The sound of musket fire at the foot of the hill, rising and falling, seemed to him like someone breathing. He listened carefully to the ebb and flow of those sounds.
"Daughter of Matthew" was the literal meaning of the name.
"Ah, breathing again, breathing!" he muttered to himself.
He pictured himself as an enormously tall, powerful man hurling cannonballs at the French with both hands.
"Come on now, Matvevna, old girl, don't let me down!" he was saying as he moved away from the gun, when a strange, unfamiliar voice called out above his head: "Captain Tushin! Captain!"
Tushin spun around, startled. It was the staff officer who had kicked him out of the booth at Grunth. The man was shouting in a breathless, gasping voice:
"Are you out of your mind? You've been ordered to retreat twice, and you..."
"Why do they have it in for me?" thought Tushin, looking up at his superior in alarm.
"I... it's not..." he stammered, raising two fingers to his cap. "I..."

But the staff officer never finished what he was saying. A cannonball whizzed so close that he ducked and folded over his horse's neck. He started to speak again, but another ball cut him short. He yanked his horse around and galloped away.
"Retreat! Everyone retreat!" he shouted from a distance.
The soldiers laughed. A moment later, another adjutant arrived with the same order.

It was Prince Andrew. The first thing he saw as he rode up to where Tushin's guns were positioned was a horse with a broken leg, unharnessed, lying beside the harnessed horses and screaming pitifully. Blood gushed from its leg like water from a spring. Among the limbers lay several dead men. One cannonball after another flew overhead as he approached, and he felt a shudder run down his spine. But the mere thought of being afraid snapped him out of it. "I cannot be afraid," he thought, and dismounted slowly among the guns. He delivered the order but did not leave the battery. He decided to stay and oversee the removal of the guns himself. Together with Tushin, stepping over the bodies and under withering French fire, he supervised the withdrawal of the cannons.
"There was a staff officer here a minute ago, but he bolted," an artilleryman said to Prince Andrew. "Not like your honor."

Prince Andrew said nothing to Tushin. They were both too absorbed in the work to seem to notice each other. When they'd managed to limber up the only two undamaged guns out of the original four and began moving downhill—leaving behind one shattered cannon and one unicorn—Prince Andrew rode up to Tushin.
"Well then, until we meet again..." he said, holding out his hand.
"Goodbye, my dear fellow," said Tushin. "Dear soul! Goodbye, my dear fellow!" And for some reason he couldn't explain, tears suddenly filled his eyes.
